One of the auxiliary subunits is the KChip protein. KChip1 is strongly expressed in RS cells and only rarely in TOR neurons. In contrast, KChip4 was largely found in TOR but not in RS cells. Further differential expression profiles were observed for DPLPs. RS cells express only DPP6L and TORs largely DPP6S. The main question is, whether minor changes in auxiliary subunit compositions indeed may underlie the significant differences in discharge patterns observed between TOR and RS cells.

1) In view of the fact that a large body of modelling experiments are based on only three TOR and two RS cells, the number of reconstructed cells plus the modelling experiments, need to be increased to 4 TOR plus 4 RS cells.

2) The observed differential expression densities of the Kv4.3 channels in RS vs TOR cells would require systematic out-side out patch recordings along the somato-dendritic domain.

3) The authors tried to block Kv4 channels with HpTx (blocks Kv4.2 and 4.3) which increased the number of APs during the initial 150 ms of a depolarizing current step in TOR cells, however, the effect was only minimal (Figure 5A/B). Since the authors argue that auxiliary subunits are important in defining the gating properties of the Kv4.3 one option would be to knock out one or the other subunit using small interference RNA. It would be great if the proposed effect of the auxiliary subunit could be further proven.

4) Can we exclude the possibility that activity states of the CCK cells may drive the expression of the auxiliary subunits? Thus, could it be that we look on the same 'class' of CCK cells of various morphologies at different 'homeostatic' plasticity states? Some CCK INs may receive a higher drive than others resulting in differential expression profiles of auxiliary subunits that 'set' their discharge patterns.

Reviewer #2:

The manuscript by Olah et al.,. is focusing on firing phenotypes of CCK-expressing interneurons in rat hippocampal CA3 area. Using a combination of whole-cell and outside-out patch-clamp recordings, patch-seq, IHC analysis and computational modelling, the authors report two firing phenotypes in the population of CCK+ cells. In particular, the low-voltage-activated delayed firing due to Kv4.3 channels and distinct Kv4 auxiliary subunits is revealed in ~50% of CCK+ cells. When put in the cell model with realistic synaptic inputs mimicking in-vivo-like conditions, this feature had impact on the cell excitability during 8-15 Hz oscillations. This work is very interesting as it demonstrates how differences in the K+ channel auxiliary subunit isoforms may affect the cell functional phenotype; it therefore brings a significant contribution to the field. However, additional analysis and text revision will be required to support the major conclusions. Specifically, additional efforts are required to (1) clarify on the cell types/identity, (2) expand the patch-seq analysis, and (3) discuss the functional significance of the observed phenomenon. Below I summarize these points:

1) Cell types/identity: the cells were identified as CCK+ based on post-hoc IHC immunolabelling. Only half of these cells exhibited the TOR firing, suggesting that there may be two different CCK+ cell sub-types. The authors put additional efforts to examine the morphological properties of recorded cells. 172 neurons were reconstructed and identified as BCs, MFAs and SC-ACs. While the TOR firing was detected in morphologically different CCK+ cell types, it would be important to validate this observation by performing cluster analysis combining electrophysiological and morphological features of recorded cells (see Hosp et al., 2014). The authors should including additional membrane properties: membrane time constant, slow AHP, Ih, rebound depolarization (e.g. CA1 CCK+ BCs and SC-ACs have different Ih and rebound depolarization, Evstratova et al., 2011)) and firing parameters (e.g., discharge frequency, ISIfirst/last, CV of ISI at different Vm levels etc.) in the cluster analysis and combine it with morphological features (e.g., axon distribution in different sublayers, dendritic features) to explore CCK+ CA3 population with TOR vs RS firing. The SC-ACs reconstructions are not illustrated in the manuscript, and, as the authors mention in the Materials and methods section, distinguishing BCs from MFA cells may be challenging due to their partially overlapping axonal termination zones. Quantitative analysis of the axon distribution is required to validate the cell identification.

2) Patch-seq analysis is prone to contamination as can be concluded from most of articles published so far using this technique (e.g., see Tripathy et al., 2018; for in-depth assessment of this issue). The authors should provide data on sample contamination before any conclusion can be made. Expression of excitatory, microglial, astrocytic and oligo markers should be shown next to the gene expression data. Negative control data from the rat CA3 region (see Luo et al., 2019) should be included. As far as I can see, cells included in patch-seq were only identified based on firing pattern and expression of Cck and Cnr1 genes. The authors should confirm the morphology of the included cells, as many interneuron types express Cck and Cnr1 genes (e.g., VIP+ subiculum-projecting cells, Luo et al., 2019). In relation to the previous point (cell identity), the authors should provide more information on gene expression by TOR vs RS cells: common vs specific genes for each firing phenotype. It is unclear how the cluster analysis of gene expression was performed (on genes detected in 3 out of 17 cells?). This analysis needs to be shown. While normalization for gene expression is a good approach, for comparison with previous published data it would be important to show the gene expression in TPM. What is shown in Figure 6A: mean +/- SE? I'm not sure that this is the right way to illustrate this data given a high variability in gene expression between individual samples. Here, the authors claim significant differences in the expression of Kv1.3, Kv3.2 and Kv4.3 genes but it is not indicated on the figure. Was it statistically significant?

3) Functional significance of two firing phenotypes within the same interneuron population (if the latter is confirmed after additional analysis) needs to be discussed more. Having two firing phenotypes within the same cell type would increase the overall variability in their firing, thus decreasing their reliability under some conditions. Under which in-vivo conditions it may happen? Do CCK+ cells exhibit a hyperpolarized Vm of -70 to -90 in vivo? What will be the network outcome given that apparently different cell types such as BCs, SC-ACs and MFAs can show this phenomenon?

Reviewer #3:

The paper by Olah et al., examines the molecular determinants of the action potential phenotype of CCK+ interneurons in the hippocampus. To address this question, the authors use electrophysiology, immunohistochemistry, single-cell RNA seq, and modeling. The main findings are:

- CCK+ interneurons in CA3 fall into two functional classes with distinct action potential phenotypes.

- Different excitability properties lead to differential recruitment of these interneurons during theta network oscillations.

- KV 4.3 contributes to the excitability in the two classes of cells, but does not explain the difference in the action potential phenotype.

- Firing properties are correlated with differential expression of Kv4 auxiliary subunits (KChIP1 vs. KChIP4e and DPP6S).

Based on these results, the authors conclude that alternative splicing of a small number of genes significantly changes the action potential phenotype of a neuron. Overall, I found this a quite nice paper. The question is interesting, the experiments are technically well performed, the results are mostly convincing, and the paper is clearly written. However, several points need to be addressed before the manuscript can be further considered.

Essential revisions:

1) The links between auxiliary subunit expression and channel function remain loose. If I read the statements correctly, (1) the effects of KChIP4e have not been investigated in recombinant expression systems, (2) it is unclear whether DPP6L and DPP6S shift the activation and inactivation curves in the proposed manner in recombinant channels, and (3) it is unclear whether ternary or higher order complexes (subsection “Same channel protein but distinct auxiliary subunits are responsible for the different ISA currents and for the different functionality of TOR and RS cells”) show the proposed properties when recombinantly expressed. Ideally, the authors should recombinantly express the proposed subunit combinations and compare the functional properties. At the very least, they should better discuss the similarities and differences between native and recombinant channels. A systematic comparison of properties in a supplementary table might help.

2) Several conclusions are based on analysis of K+ currents in the whole-cell voltage-clamp configuration. However, voltage-clamp errors may be a problem in these measurements. At the very least, they should better discuss this point. Additionally, pharmacological isolation of Kv4 currents in high TEA concentrations might be useful to improve voltage clamp.

3) Activation and inactivation curves of several ion channels are known to be affected by patch configuration and time-dependent changes, e.g. shifts to more negative values over time (Donnan effects may contribute to these changes). This raises the question whether the curves were similar in different recording configurations and affected by nonstationarities. At the very least, statements should be added to the Methods section.

4) The authors conclude that fine-tuning in gating and conductance density of K+ channels is critically important for determining the action potential phenotype. This seems in contrast to the previous demonstration that the same firing pattern can be generated by several combinations of conductances (Marder and Goaillard, 2006). The authors should better discuss these opposing views.

5) The evidence for an involvement of alternatively spliced auxiliary subunits is compelling but remains correlative. The authors should clearly mention the limitations of the correlative approach in both Abstract and Discussion section.

6) The modeling section is unclear. Inclusion of a table with the main free parameters may provide the necessary clarification. Furthermore, the Materials and methods section addressing this part needs to be rewritten. Finally, it is not entirely clear whether two populations of channels are indeed required to describe ISA channel gating in TOR cells. A single population with intermediate gating properties may do the same job.

7) Surely, mRNA and protein expression are important, but acute modifications (e.g. by phosphorylation) may be also relevant. At the very least, appropriate caveat sentences should be added.

8) Finally, the paper is too long in relation to the novel information it contains. It should be shortened to approximately 60 to 70%. A scheme of the proposed mechanisms at the end of the paper might increase clarity and help in shortening the text.

results.result: Two distinct firing phenotypes of CCK+INs exist in rat hippocampal CA3: TOR cells (n=290) showing membrane potential-dependent firing with delayed onset (252±15 ms from hyperpolarized potentials) and RS cells (n=267) showing regular firing with short delays (33±2 ms). Both phenotypes are stable over prolonged recordings and show similar firing from depolarized potentials.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C24-C34 provide converging evidence from 557 recorded cells with detailed quantitative measurements, statistical analyses, and voltage-dependence characterization (V1/2 values, Boltzmann fits with R²>0.99). The stability over 45-64 min recordings (C34) confirms these are intrinsic properties rather than recording artifacts.

results.result: TOR and RS cells show similar basic electrophysiological properties (input resistance, AP threshold, half-width, rate of rise, after-hyperpolarization, spontaneous synaptic events) and are present in both young and adult rats, suggesting the firing phenotypes are not age-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 report quantitative measurements with statistical comparisons showing no significant differences in basic properties. Claims C38-C39 demonstrate presence in adult rats (>70 days), though the inference about age-independence (C39) is based on presence rather than developmental tracking.

results.result: TOR and RS firing phenotypes do not correlate with previously established morphological subtypes of CCK+INs (basket cells, mossy fiber-associated, Schaffer collateral-associated cells), as both firing types occur similarly across all three morphological categories.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 provide morphological classification of 172 cells with distribution data (Figure 2B) showing both firing types across all morphological subtypes. This is further supported by quantitative morphological analyses (Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2) referenced in C114.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing of 8 TOR and 8 RS cells reveals highly similar overall transcriptomic profiles (3000+ genes detected), with most CCK+IN marker genes expressed comparably. However, Satb1 and Lypd1 show differential expression, with Satb1 being predictive of TOR identity (present in all TOR cells vs. 4/8 RS cells, p=0.0095).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C49 provide RNA-seq data with appropriate quality metrics and statistical analyses. The hierarchical cluster analysis (C48) failing to separate the groups supports the similarity claim. However, the small sample size (n=8 per group) and the fact that Satb1 was only present in 4/8 RS cells (not 0/8) suggests some overlap between groups.

results.result: Immunohistochemical validation confirms RNA-seq findings: CB1R, VGluT3, Reelin, and Calb1 proteins occur similarly in both cell types, while Satb1 protein is predominantly found in TOR cells (82.6% of TOR vs. 10.9% of RS cells). Satb1 expression in non-recorded CCK+ cells (126/425 in CA3) confirms this is not a recording artifact.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 provide immunohistochemical validation with large sample sizes (>100 cells per group for Satb1). The concordance between RNA-seq and protein data strengthens the findings, and the analysis of non-recorded cells (C54) addresses potential recording-induced artifacts.

results.result: TOR cells exhibit larger low-voltage-activated potassium currents (ISA) at firing threshold (683±109 pA vs. 148±28 pA in RS cells, p=0.0006) with left-shifted voltage dependence of inactivation (V1/2: -64.5 mV vs. -57.4 mV, p=0.0006) and slower inactivation kinetics (71.2±9.1 ms vs. 18.8±1.7 ms, p=0.0007).
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 provide comprehensive voltage-clamp characterization with appropriate statistical comparisons, sample sizes (n=11-17), and high-quality Boltzmann fits (R²=0.999). The measurements are internally consistent and explain the functional differences between cell types.

results.result: Nucleated patch recordings reveal that despite lower ISA density in TOR cells (1.91±0.46 nS/pF vs. 3.86±0.8 nS/pF in RS), the left-shifted activation and slower inactivation result in larger inhibitory charge during physiologically relevant voltage steps (0.47±0.1 vs. 0.21±0.05 pC/pF, p=0.032).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 provide nucleated patch data with statistical analyses. The apparent paradox (lower density but larger functional effect) is resolved by the kinetic differences, demonstrating sophisticated understanding of channel biophysics. However, the small sample sizes (n=7-8) warrant caution.

results.result: Outside-out patch recordings confirm higher somatic ISA density in RS cells (70.5±15.2 vs. 42.2±5.2 pA/µm², p=0.047) but similar dendritic density (19.6±3.3 vs. 19.5±3.0 pA/µm²) with no distance-dependent gradient. TOR cells show pronounced patch-to-patch variability in ISA kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 provide detailed subcellular localization data with large sample sizes (n=47-56 patches). The lack of dendritic gradient (C70) is supported by appropriate statistical analyses (R²=0.01-0.011, p>0.2). The variability observation (C71) is descriptive but consistent with clustered channel distribution.

results.result: Pharmacological experiments demonstrate that Kv4-mediated currents are crucial for the TOR phenomenon: HpTX (1 µM) reversibly shortened the delay of first APs in TOR cells from 239±61 ms to 116±38 ms (p=0.01) and increased early firing, while having no effect on RS cells. Neither TEA nor low-dose 4-AP eliminated the TOR phenomenon.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C78 provide systematic pharmacological characterization with appropriate controls, reversibility testing, and statistical analyses. The selective effect of HpTX on TOR cells (C75-C76) with no effect on RS cells (C77) strongly supports the mechanistic interpretation (C78).

results.result: Both TOR and RS cells contain substantial HpTX-sensitive (Kv4-mediated) currents, but with different properties: TOR cell currents activate at more negative voltages, have slower inactivation (49.1±12.6 ms vs. 11.8±1.6 ms), and show left-shifted voltage dependence of inactivation (V1/2: -64.0±0.6 mV vs. -56.8±1.3 mV).
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 provide detailed pharmacological characterization of HpTX-sensitive currents with quantitative measurements and appropriate sample sizes (n=7 per group). The conclusion (C82) that Kv4 channels mediate ISA in both cell types is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Computational modeling demonstrates that swapping ISA conductance properties alone (ISARS to ISATOR+RS) is sufficient to convert RS to TOR firing phenotype in the same reconstructed cells. TOR firing requires 57.9% less total ISA conductance than RS firing (1.72±0.27 vs. 2.97±0.47 mS/cm²).
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84, C115-C116 describe realistic computational models using 10 reconstructed cells with detailed morphology and known conductances. The sufficiency demonstration (swapping single conductance converts phenotype) is compelling, though the models rely on assumptions about conductance distributions and parameters.

results.result: Computational simulations predict that TOR cells are selectively silenced during 8-15 Hz oscillatory inputs (37.2±0.4% fewer APs compared to RS configuration) but show only minor differences at lower (1-6 Hz) and higher (25-100 Hz) frequencies. Under basal conditions, TOR cells are unlikely to contribute to theta oscillations unless primed by preceding depolarizations.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 provide quantitative modeling results with physiologically relevant input patterns. The frequency-selective silencing is well-demonstrated in Figure 4D. However, the predictions (C4, C108-C109) require in vivo validation, and the models make assumptions about synaptic input patterns that may not fully capture in vivo complexity.

results.result: Kv4.3 mRNA is detected in most CCK+INs (15/16 cells) with comparable expression levels between TOR and RS cells (1.56±0.34 vs. 2.03±0.4, p=0.37). Immunohistochemistry confirms Kv4.3 protein presence in both cell types (15/20 TOR, 19/23 RS), but with stronger signal in RS cells, consistent with higher channel density.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90, C92-C94, C117 provide convergent RNA-seq and immunohistochemical evidence. The paradox that RS cells have more Kv4.3 despite TOR cells showing the distinctive Kv4-dependent phenotype is acknowledged and explained by auxiliary subunit differences. The immunohistochemistry is qualitative ('usually stronger') rather than quantitative.

results.result: KChIP1 is differentially expressed between cell types: detected in most RS cells (6/8 by RNA-seq, 20/27 by immunohistochemistry) but absent or low in TOR cells (3/8 RNA-seq, 5/21 immunohistochemistry; p=0.025 for RNA). KChIP1 is known to increase Kv4 surface expression and accelerate inactivation kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97, C101 provide convergent RNA-seq and immunohistochemical evidence with statistical support. The functional interpretation (C119-C120) relies on literature citations rather than direct experimental validation in this system. The overlap between groups (KChIP1 present in some TOR cells) suggests this is not an absolute determinant.

results.result: TOR cells primarily express the KChIP4e isoform (7/8 cells), a transmembrane KChIP that does not facilitate Kv4 surface expression and confers slow inactivation kinetics, while RS cells express KChIP1. This differential expression of auxiliary subunit isoforms underlies the distinct ISA properties and firing phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 provide exon-level RNA-seq analysis identifying specific isoforms. The mechanistic interpretation (C102, C123) integrates the molecular data with functional properties and literature on KChIP4e function (C121-C122). However, direct functional validation of KChIP4e effects in this system is lacking, and the immunohistochemistry for KChIP4 was largely negative (contradicting RNA data).

results.result: DPP10c is ubiquitously expressed in both cell types, while DPP6 isoforms differ: RS cells primarily express DPP6L, whereas TOR cells express DPP6S (7/8 cells) and/or DPP6L (4/8 cells). DPP6S may contribute to the left-shifted voltage dependence of activation in TOR cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 provide isoform-level RNA-seq analysis. The functional interpretation (C124) regarding DPP6S effects is based on literature rather than direct validation. The presence of both DPP6S and DPP6L in some TOR cells complicates the interpretation, and the relative contributions of different DPLP isoforms remain unclear.

results.result: The distinct firing phenotypes and functional properties of TOR and RS cells are established by alternative splicing of a few auxiliary subunit genes (KChIP1 vs. KChIP4e, DPP6L vs. DPP6S), representing a minor change in the whole transcriptome that determines cell-type identity.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C125, C118 synthesize the molecular and functional findings into a coherent model. The evidence from RNA-seq, immunohistochemistry, electrophysiology, pharmacology, and modeling converges to support this conclusion. However, direct causal validation (e.g., manipulating auxiliary subunit expression to convert cell types) is not provided, and the relative contributions of different auxiliary subunits remain incompletely resolved.

results.result: The different excitability properties destine TOR and RS cells for distinct functions during network oscillations. The TOR phenomenon potentially explains variable recruitment of individual CCK+INs during theta cycles, and the elimination of bursts in TOR cells during theta is expected to diminish GABAergic inhibition from this subset onto CA3 neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C110, C112 make functional predictions based on modeling and known CCK+IN properties (C111 from literature). While the modeling is rigorous (C85-C87), these functional interpretations require in vivo validation. The predictions are plausible but speculative (C110 uses 'potentially'), and alternative explanations for variable CCK+IN recruitment are not excluded.

results.result: Despite their functional distinction, TOR and RS cells have surprisingly similar general intrinsic excitability, morphology, and gene expression profiles, and cannot be distinguished by standard transcriptomic or morphological cell-type classification approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C113-C114 are supported by comprehensive characterization including electrophysiology (C35-C36), morphology (C40-C42, Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2), and RNA-seq (C48-C49). The cluster analyses failing to separate the groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) provide strong support. This challenges conventional cell-type definitions.
